you're activation patterns are poo. Sounds like you have some anterior pelvic tilt going on, and whatever other compensations bodywide to go with it. Here are some simple tests:

  • lay completely flat on the ground, with your arms above your head. externally rotate your shoulders, making your palms face the ceiling as much as they can. No one should be able to slide a hand under your lower back. Now without collapsing the chest (keep the chin tucked and neck neutral, shoulders back chest up,) bring your knees towards your chest and your arms under your feet. Lay out completely flat to end the rep, with arms above the head again. When you layout your arms above your head. This is called a tuck-up, and its a very high standard, but one of the most basic exercises in gymnastic conditioning. If you simply cannot get into the starting position of being layed-out with low back on the ground, that's test enough.

-Test your ankle dorsiflexion. With a straight leg (tight butt, and tight vastus medialis, the teardrop shaped quad that's on the inside of the leg,) place your toes on the wall, heel on the ground, and try to bring the top of your foot to your shin. If you're under 10 degrees (even more is ideal) here you have lots of work to do on your calves and feet, which can present their issues in the hamstrings, and almost also go hand in hand with hamstring issues in the first place. Do not move your back around to cheat this stretch, keep a neutral spine.

-Do you have a butt? I doubt it. Have standards here, don't think your tiny tight tush is good enough. You want to get as close to a Sidney Crosby/Latina honey ass as possible. https://www.t-nation.com/training/dispelling-the-glute-myth everyone can use more glute training, as they are s'posed to be the largest muscles on your body (maximus in particular.)

Although my two tests are not super amazing, they should help to get realistic about problems. Check your ankle mobility, check your pelvis control. You need and ankle which is capable of squatting, and a pelvis that can find its endrange in posterior tilt, as a man your pelvis should rest at 0 degrees, so over training posterior tilt should help it rebound back to 0. Glute training is going to be vital if you do have the ATP (and still necessary otherwise) as most of it will be done in a posterior tilt of the pelvis. Also, it goes without saying, tight butts, tight guts, which is the main part of addressing the weak abdominal present in overactive hamstrings. Stretching the hamstrings is usually highly ineffective until the system is being address, and then it still goes hand in hand with working feet and stretching your calves also.
